title: Confined space entry — fire water tanks, pump wells, pits and risers
verdict:
I would not sign this and send a crew out on it today — but it is two additions away from being the best confined space statement I have read for this trade, and nothing in it is dishonest.

WHAT IS WRONG (two serious, both fatal omissions rather than errors)

1. Nothing controls ignition in a flammable atmosphere the work itself creates. steps[9] names solvent-based lining and re-coating as a hazard, then controls it with ventilation, continuous monitoring and RPE. The only ignition control anywhere in the document is the hot work permit. Meanwhile the document directs an ELV head torch, battery tools, a mains sump pump and an electric blower into the space — all shock and water controls, none of them intrinsically safe. WHS Reg s 73 is cited in references[10] and implemented nowhere. Verbatim: 'a person conducting a business or undertaking must ensure that an ignition source is not introduced into a confined space (from outside or within the space) if there is a possibility of the ignition source causing a fire or explosion in the space.'

2. The space itself is never assessed for collapse. steps[3] control 2 endorses draining one cell of a multi-cell tank while the other stays in service — correct fire-protection practice, and it puts full one-sided head on a dividing wall with the entrant standing on the dry side. The control isolates and blanks the balance line and never asks whether the wall is rated for that. Nor does anything require the tank vent to be confirmed clear before draw-down, or the corroded internals, tie rods and panel joints to be assessed for collapse onto the entrant — they appear only as a head-strike hazard. This document controls every way the space can hurt the entrant except the space itself falling in.

Six minor findings follow: fall arrest labelled engineering at steps[8] controls[1] (s 79(3)(c) makes it the last resort), a measure-the-opening hold point labelled isolate at steps[7] controls[0], the aspirated sampling pump and hose that steps[6] requires never appearing on the steps[0] load-out list, a probable CPCWHS1001 / CPCCWHS1001 unit code slip I could not settle against training.gov.au, three unnamed hazards (snakes in pits, suspension intolerance, manual handling of the rescue plant), and two small over-statements of s 37 and BFSR s 49.

WHAT IS RIGHT, AND I CHECKED ALL OF IT

Every legal citation in this document is correct. I pulled the WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld), the WHS Act 2011 (Qld), the Electrical Safety Act 2002 (Qld), the Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) and the Fire Services Act 1990 (Qld) in force today from legislation.qld.gov.au and read them.

- hrcw: s 291(a), (d), (f), (k), (l), (n), (o), (q) — all eight quoted verbatim against the current text, punctuation aside.
- Part 4.3: ss 62(1)(c), 66(2)(3)(5), 67(1)(2)(a)(4), 68, 69, 71(1)(b), 71(2)(a)(b), 72(2), 74(1)(b)(2)(3)(a)(b)(c), 75(2)(3), 76(2), 77(2)(3) — every one exists, and every one says what the document says it says. The hard readings are right: s 71(2) really does make a safe oxygen level the primary duty with air supply as a fallback only below 19.5%, and there really is no fallback for enrichment above 23.5%. The 5%/10% LEL removal rules in s 72(2) are quoted accurately.
- Schedule 19: confined space definition and safe oxygen level (19.5%-23.5%) confirmed.
- Chapter 6: ss 289(2)(e), 289(3)(d), 290(2), 299(2)(d), 299(4), 300, 302, 303(1)(2)(3)(4) all confirmed. The whenRequired note that Part 4.3 stands on its own footing regardless of the Chapter 6 argument is legally sound and well put.
- WHS Act ss 35, 36(c), 37, 38, 39 confirmed.
- Electrical Safety Act s 18(1)(b) confirmed: electrical work includes 'testing ... electrical equipment or an electrical installation'. The line drawn — technician switches and locks, licensed worker proves dead — holds against the section.
- Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) is SL 2008 No. 160 and is still in force. ss 49, 50, 53, 54 confirmed, including the 24-hour critical defect notice being a duty on the person who did the maintenance, and the pump-defect example being the Regulation's own.
- Fire Services Act 1990 s 233 confirmed word for word, and QFR is the correct current name.
- The repealed Electrical Safety Regulation 2013 appears exactly once, in references[21], correctly described as replaced. The Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 Part 8 Division 3 citation at steps[3] is the live one.

Every standard checks out on the Standards Australia record, including the ones I expected to find invented: AS/NZS 1891.4:2025 is real and Current (superseding the 2009 edition and its Amd 1:2021); AS 1674.1:2025 is real and Current (superseding AS 1674.1-1997); AS/NZS 2865:2009 is Pending Revision with Amendment 1:2025, exactly as stated; AS 2118.1:2017 carries Amd 1:2017, 2:2020 and 3:2024; AS/NZS 3000:2018 carries Amd 1:2020, 2:2021 and 3:2023. AS 1851-2012, AS 2419.1:2021, AS 2941-2013, AS 2304:2019, AS/NZS 1891.1:2020, AS/NZS 1715:2009, AS/NZS 1716:2012 and AS/NZS ISO 16975.3:2023 all confirmed under those numbers with those titles.

Could not verify, and not counted against the document: the Code of Practice titles and years, and the 1300 362 128 notification number. worksafe.qld.gov.au sits behind a Cloudflare challenge that returns 403 to everything from this session. Nothing in them looked wrong.

JSON SHAPE: exact. Twelve keys, no extras, no omissions, no suggestFor, id preserved as 'confined-space'. All thirteen steps order controls highest-first with no violations, no residual risk exceeds its initial risk, and no step relies on administrative or PPE alone at a low residual — the two low-residual steps (steps[0] planning and steps[10] exit) each carry a real higher-order control.

USABILITY: a competent three-person crew could work to this, and the document is honest about the cost of that — it says out loud that a two-man run does not go ahead, that a missing ticket reschedules the job, and that an entry with no riggable on-site retrieval does not happen. The heat rotation regime, the LEL sensor warning, the rear-D retrieval warning and the refill hold point are the writing of somebody who has been in these tanks. Fix the ignition control and the structural assessment and I would sign it.

blocking.field: steps[9] "Do the work inside the space" — controls array (and steps[5] control 'ELV IP-rated' lighting)
blocking.problem: FATAL OMISSION — no ignition-source control for a flammable atmosphere the work itself creates. The step names the hazards 'Airborne contaminant generated by the work itself — solvent-based lining or re-coating' and 'Hot work igniting a flammable atmosphere, a tank liner or accumulated sludge', but the ONLY ignition control in the whole document is the hot work permit. Solvent-based tank lining or re-coating fills a steel tank with vapour in the explosive range, and the document positively directs non-hot-work ignition sources into that space: 'ELV IP-rated head torch' (steps[5] and ppe), 'Battery tools instead of 240V leads' (steps[9]), a mains sump pump 'powered from outside on an RCD', and an electric blower. ELV, IP-rated, RCD-protected and battery-powered are all shock and water controls — none of them means intrinsically safe (Ex ia) or non-sparking. Nothing requires intrinsically safe lighting and instruments, non-sparking tools, bonding and earthing of the sprayer and drums, or removal of the blower motor from the vapour path. The document cites Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 73 in references[10] but no step implements it. s 73 reads: 'A person conducting a business or undertaking must ensure that an ignition source is not introduced into a confined space (from outside or within the space) if there is a possibility of the ignition source causing a fire or explosion in the space. Maximum penalty—60 penalty units.' The document also correctly warns twice that oxygen enrichment 'turns a rusty tank into a bomb' — and then leaves the bomb without an ignition control.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[9], above the existing substitute control: an 'eliminate' control barring solvent-based lining, coating and solvent cleaning from confined space entry work under this SWMS (send it to a coatings SWMS with its own hazardous-atmosphere assessment); and an 'isolate' control for anything that proceeds — every item taken into or run at the space certified intrinsically safe for the vapour, blower motor and starter kept outside and clear of the vapour path, spray equipment and drums bonded and earthed, no hot surfaces, and continuous LEL monitoring with automatic withdrawal at 5% LEL (s 72(2), already cited correctly at steps[6]). Name Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 73 in the control text, not only in references.

blocking.field: steps[3] "Isolate, lock and tag every service connected to the space" — control 2 (level 'isolate', multi-cell tanks); and the absence of any drain/draw-down step between steps[3] and steps[4]
blocking.problem: FATAL OMISSION — the structural integrity of the space itself is never assessed, and the document endorses the exact practice that loads it. steps[3] control 2 says: 'Draining one cell while the other stays in service to keep the building protected is how this work is normally done'. Emptying one cell of a twin-cell bolted or panel tank puts full one-sided hydrostatic head on a dividing wall that in many fire tanks was designed for balanced cells, and the entrant is standing on the dry side of it. The control addresses only the water path (isolate and blank the balance line, overflow and cross-connection) — it never asks whether the dividing wall is rated for differential head, and never requires that question to go to the tank manufacturer, the site's engineer or the AS 2304 documentation. Two related gaps sit with it: (a) nothing anywhere requires the tank vent or breather to be confirmed clear before the tank is drained or pumped down — a fire tank drawn down against a blocked vent collapses inward, and steps[9] runs a sump pump for the whole entry; (b) the corroded condition of internals, tie rods, roof supports and panel joints appears only as a head-strike hazard in steps[8], never as a collapse risk onto a person inside, even though steps[8] already accepts that fire tank steelwork 'sit[s] in wet chlorinated air for decades and go[es] at the fixings' and steps[4] accepts that panel roofs 'give way at the panel joint'. The document is otherwise rigorous about every way the space can hurt the entrant except the space falling in on them.
blocking.fix: Add a drain and draw-down step before steps[4], or controls within steps[3]: an 'administrative' HOLD POINT confirming, from the tank documentation or the manufacturer, that any dividing wall between a drained cell and a cell left in service is rated for full one-sided head — and where that cannot be confirmed, both cells come down together and the impairment is planned around it; an 'engineering' control confirming the vent/breather and overflow are clear and stay clear for the whole draw-down, with a controlled drain rate; and an 'administrative' control adding a structural walk-around of internals, tie rods, roof supports and panel joints to the pre-entry inspection, with visible distortion, rust-through at a fixing or a sprung panel joint as a NO ENTRY and a defect to report.

blocking.problem: Control-hierarchy mislabel of exactly the kind this document otherwise avoids. The control reads 'Fall arrest for the descent: retrieval line under tension on the winch, or a self-retracting device rated for the fall distance and for rescue, anchored to the tripod or to a rated anchor' and is labelled engineering. A personal fall arrest system is the last resort in the falls hierarchy, below fall prevention devices and work positioning systems — Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 79(3) ranks them (a) fall prevention device, (b) work positioning system, (c) fall arrest system. Labelling it engineering tells a reader the step leads with a higher-order control than it has. steps[4] controls[3] has the milder version of the same problem: restraint on a rated anchor is a work positioning system under s 79(3)(b), not engineering. The control text is right in both places; only the level is wrong.
blocking.fix: Relabel steps[8] controls[1] to 'ppe' and move it below the administrative controls so the ordering rule still holds; the tripod, davit and rated anchor themselves can stay as a separate 'engineering' control. For steps[4] controls[3], either relabel to 'ppe' or reword so the engineering element (the rated anchor and its documentation) is the control and the harness and line are named as the PPE that attaches to it.

blocking.field: steps[7] "Issue the entry permit and set the crew, standby, retrieval and comms" — controls[0], level 'isolate'
blocking.problem: A verification hold point labelled as an isolation. 'HOLD POINT — measure the opening. Write its dimensions and shape on the permit. Confirm with the gear in your hands that the retrieval device and a casualty in a harness with retrieval straps will physically pass through it...' isolates nothing — it is a stop/go check, and it is the first control in the step, so the step reads as though it opens with an isolation. This is the same failure mode as calling a permit an isolation. The substance is excellent and the s 74(3)(a) and (b) citation is correct and verified.
blocking.fix: Relabel to 'administrative' and move it below the two engineering controls (the rigged tripod/winch and the comms), keeping the HOLD POINT emphasis in the text.

blocking.field: steps[0] "Plan the job and check the gear before leaving the yard" — controls[1] (the load-out list), and the ppe array
blocking.problem: Usability gap between the method and the packing list. steps[6] requires 'Test from outside the space with a sampling pump and hose' and readings 'at the top, at mid-depth and at the bottom', with hose draw time allowed at each depth. Neither the yard load-out in steps[0] controls[1] nor the ppe array ever names an aspirated sampling pump, sample hose or probe, or spare tubing — the only instrument named anywhere is the 'Personal 4-gas monitor', which the document itself correctly describes as a diffusion warning device. A crew that packs to this list arrives unable to perform the pre-entry test the permit turns on, and the shortcut it invites is the one steps[6] bans in the same breath ('Nobody puts their head in to take a reading').
blocking.fix: Add the aspirated sampling pump or pumped 4-gas instrument, the sample hose long enough to reach the bottom of the deepest space on the run, the probe and spare tubing, and the bump test gas, to the steps[0] load-out list, and note the hose draw time (roughly 2-3 seconds per metre plus instrument response) on the permit alongside the readings.

blocking.field: training[10] — "CPCWHS1001 Prepare to work safely in the construction industry (white card)"
blocking.problem: Probable wrong national unit code. Units in the CPC Construction, Plumbing and Services training package carry a four-letter CPCC prefix, and the white card unit is CPCCWHS1001, not CPCWHS1001. I could not settle this against training.gov.au from this session — the site would not serve page content through the proxy (the SPA returns an empty shell and the payload endpoint returns 32 bytes), so I am flagging it for confirmation rather than asserting it. Every other training code in the array (RIIWHS202E, RIIWHS204E, MSMWHS217, PUASAR025, HLTAID011, HLTAID009) is consistent with its training package's naming and I found nothing against them.
blocking.fix: Confirm on training.gov.au and correct to 'CPCCWHS1001 Prepare to work safely in the construction industry (white card)' if that is what the National Register shows. The obligation is unambiguous either way, so this is a records-accuracy fix, not a safety one.

blocking.field: steps[9] hazards array (and steps[1] hazards) — hazards not named anywhere in the document
blocking.problem: Three foreseeable hazards on this specific work are not named at all: (1) snakes and vermin in below-ground valve pits, booster pits and wet wells — a genuine Queensland killer in exactly these spaces, and absent from every hazard list; (2) suspension intolerance / orthostatic shock where an entrant is arrested on the descent or left hanging after retrieval — the emergency section gets the casualty out fast, which mitigates it, but the condition is never named and neither is the instruction not to lay a suspended casualty flat too quickly; (3) manual handling of the tripod, winch, blower and ducting onto a roof or across a car park, which is the most likely injury on the day even though it is not the most severe.
blocking.fix: Add the snake/vermin hazard to steps[1] and steps[5] with a control (probe and look before reaching in, torch the space from outside, gaiters and gloves, stop work and call the site if there is an animal in the space). Add suspension intolerance to steps[8] hazards with the retrieval-time expectation and post-retrieval handling in emergency. Add a manual-handling line to steps[4].

blocking.field: emergency ("WHAT HAS TO BE NOTIFIED" paragraph), and steps[11] controls[5] (critical defect notice)
blocking.problem: Two small over-statements of what a verified source says. (1) The emergency section lists, as s 37 dangerous incidents, 'an isolation that failed, an entrant who had to be retrieved and walked away fine'. Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (Qld) s 37 is a closed list of exposures — paragraphs (a) to (l), covering uncontrolled escape/spillage/leakage of a substance, uncontrolled implosion/explosion/fire, uncontrolled escape of gas or steam, escape of a pressurised substance, electric shock, fall or release from a height of plant/substance/thing, and so on, plus '(l) any other event prescribed under a regulation'. A failed isolation or an uninjured retrieval is not squarely in that list unless it involved one of those exposures. The document's instruction to over-notify is safe and I would not change it — but attributing those two examples to s 37 states the section as saying something it does not. (2) steps[11] controls[5] paraphrases the Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) s 49 test as a defect 'reasonably likely to have a significant adverse impact on the safety of occupants if a fire happens'. s 49(b) actually reads '...if a fire or hazardous materials emergency happens' — the paraphrase narrows the statutory trigger.
blocking.fix: In emergency, keep both examples but present them as house practice: 'a failed isolation and an uninjured retrieval both get rung in as a matter of Safe QLD practice, and they are usually notifiable in their own right because of what the entrant was exposed to'. In steps[11] controls[5], restore 'if a fire or hazardous materials emergency happens'.
